newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan takes wary step toward approving the pill.
newsitem.headline: Japan takes wary step toward approving the pill.

text.p: Japan moved a hesitant step closer to approving the birth control pill on Monday after a key government committee on public health softened its negative stance towards oral contraceptives.

The committee's conclusion that the pill's approval could help spread AIDS and other sexually transmitted diseases angered many who believe the issues should be kept separate, but there were also sighs of relief that the committee did not oppose the pill outright.
"We have progressed an important step. The committee's report can now be read as saying that it is OK to approve the pill," said a spokesman for a pharmaceutical firm who declined to be named.

The public health committee worried women's groups and pharmaceutical firms when, at its meeting last month, some members said they were against removing the ban because it may discourage condom use and help spread AIDS.
Officials also said the committee's conclusion, which called for a wide-ranging public awareness campaign about effective condom use, was not negative.
"The committee doesn't want to be understood as having given the pill the go-sign, but it was not a negative opinion," said a Health Ministry official.
Japan remains the only major country in the world to ban the pill for contraceptive purposes, more than 30 years after it was introduced in the West.
The low-dose pill is banned altogether, while high- and medium-dose pills can only be prescribed for menstrual disorders.

The pill has gone through tortuous cycles of coming within inches of official approval before being turned back. Concerns over sexual mores, possible pill side effects and AIDS have all played their part, as have ignorance and indifference.
Monday's public health committee meeting, however, drew a crowd of 100 women observers, the largest show of support for the pill by Japanese women in recent years.
The pill will now be discussed by the Health Ministry's Pharmaceutical Council, in effect the last major hurdle it has to clear before receiving an official blessing.
Despite renewed optimism that approval may come this year, many were still vocal in their criticism of the public health committee and the direction it was trying to take.
They charged that it is using the pill to push its own agenda on sexually transmitted diseases and that, with only two women and no gynecologists as members, it did not reflect the concerns of women.

"For example, suggestions from the committee that tests for sexually transmitted diseases be recommended for pill users seemed to say that they were aiming for the pill not to be used," said Midori Ashida, a writer who attended the meeting.
The committee's view that the pill should always be combined with condoms was also criticised.
"If you have a steady partner whom you trust, then it should be enough to just use the pill," said a spokesman for another pharmaceutical firm.
